title: Global Institutions and Continuity and Change
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: The United Nations, founded in 1945 as World War II ended, was a second attempt at the dream of the failed League of Nations: a permanent forum where nearly every country could meet, debate, and cooperate to keep the peace, defend human rights, and address common problems.

As the world grew more interconnected, problems increasingly spilled across national borders — war, disease, economic crises, environmental damage, and human-rights abuses — and no single nation could solve them alone, driving the rise of international institutions to govern shared challenges.

The United Nations provided a forum for diplomacy, organized peacekeeping missions, and spawned a family of specialized agencies, becoming the central institution of attempted global governance despite real limits on its power.

The World Health Organization (WHO), a specialized UN agency, coordinated global health campaigns, including the worldwide vaccination effort that eradicated smallpox by 1980 and ongoing efforts to fight disease across the planet.

The global economy was governed by institutions including the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which lent money and shaped policy, and the World Trade Organization (WTO), which set the rules of global commerce.

The European Union was the most ambitious regional organization, building a common market, a shared currency (the euro) for many members, and supranational institutions among historic enemies who had fought two world wars, knitting nations more tightly together.

Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) such as Amnesty International (human rights), Doctors Without Borders (medical aid), and Greenpeace (environment) became powerful global actors, operating across borders to pursue causes independently of governments.

Beyond governments and NGOs, powerful multinational corporations became major global actors in their own right, operating across borders to pursue profits and sometimes wielding more economic power than the governments meant to regulate them.

International institutions achieved real things: coordinating disease eradication, providing humanitarian relief, setting trade rules, advancing human-rights norms, and helping keep the peace in many places, extending globalization into the realm of politics and governance.

The central political tension of the contemporary world is between the pull toward global integration and cooperation and the enduring power of the sovereign nation-state, which guards its sovereignty and pursues its own interests.

Despite all the integration of the global age, the nation-state has not withered away. Nations jealously guard their sovereignty, pursue their own interests, and frequently refuse to be bound by international institutions when it suits them.

Global institutions are limited by national sovereignty: the UN can be paralyzed by the vetoes and rivalries of powerful states, climate agreements depend on nations voluntarily keeping promises they often break, and international law has no reliable means of enforcement against a defiant powerful state.

The persistence and recent resurgence of nationalism in many countries, partly as a backlash against globalization, shows the continuing grip of national identity and sovereignty even in a deeply interconnected world.

The deepest challenges of the global age — climate change above all, but also pandemics, financial crises, migration, and weapons of mass destruction — are global problems that demand global cooperation, yet the world remains organized into roughly two hundred sovereign nation-states with no world government to compel it.

A model synthesis traces networks of exchange across the whole course: the Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, and trans-Saharan routes (Units 1–2), the Columbian Exchange connecting hemispheres (Unit 4), the industrial world economy (Units 5–6), and modern global supply chains (Units 7–9), revealing a deep continuity of growing connection.

The change in networks of exchange over time was dramatic in scale and speed: Silk Roads goods took years to cross Eurasia, but today money crosses the planet in milliseconds; a disease once spread along caravan routes over decades now circles the globe by airplane in weeks; networks grew from regional to hemispheric to planetary.

A continuity-and-change argument names a fundamental pattern that persisted across the whole span (continuity), traces how the theme transformed across eras with specific cross-regional evidence (change), and builds a thesis that holds both together and explains their relationship.

Synthesis is the capstone skill of connecting developments across many regions and eras to reveal continuity and change. The most powerful LEQ strategy is to choose one course theme and run it across the whole span with specific evidence from multiple eras and regions.

Major through-line themes of the course include networks of exchange (Silk Roads to global supply chains), state-building (land empires to nation-states to international institutions), technology (gunpowder to industrial machines to the internet), social hierarchies (caste/feudal to industrial class to global inequality), the environment (agriculture to industrialization to climate change), and belief/culture (world religions to the Enlightenment to global culture and its backlash).

The United Nations represents a continuity with the failed League of Nations: it was a second, stronger attempt to build global governance after WWII, learning from the League's weaknesses while still being limited by the sovereignty of powerful member states.

The course traces humanity's journey from a world of separate regions loosely linked by caravan and sailing ship in 1200 to a single, instantaneously interconnected world of nearly eight billion people facing shared crises no nation can solve alone, organized still into competing sovereign nation-states.
